content: Community health workers (CHWs) have no direct evidence supporting their ability to provide certain abortion-related services. However, indirect evidence suggests that CHWs can effectively use simple tools and checklists to determine gestational age based on patient history and assess eligibility for and outcomes of medical abortion with low to moderate certainty. CHWs are often involved in counseling women seeking abortion care, and their interventions are generally acceptable and feasible in various settings. The skills required for managing incomplete abortion with misoprostol are similar to those needed for providing medical abortion at less than 12 weeks of gestation, a task recommended for CHWs. Traditional and complementary medicine professionals have low-certainty evidence supporting their safety and effectiveness in providing medical abortion at gestational ages under 12 weeks. Their skills for managing incomplete abortion with misoprostol are comparable to those required for medical abortion provision. Auxiliary nurses and auxiliary nurse midwives (ANMs) have moderate-certainty evidence supporting their safety and effectiveness in providing medical abortion at gestational ages under 12 weeks. Their skills for managing incomplete abortion with misoprostol are also similar. This option is feasible and has the potential to increase equitable access to quality abortion care. Nurses have moderate-certainty indirect evidence supporting their safety, effectiveness, and acceptability in providing medical abortion. Their skills for managing incomplete abortion with misoprostol are comparable. This option is feasible and could enhance equitable access to quality abortion care. Midwives have moderateto high-certainty evidence from low-resource settings supporting their safety and effectiveness in managing incomplete abortion. Women report high satisfaction with midwives as providers. This option is feasible and has the potential to improve equitable access to quality abortion care. Associate and advanced associate clinicians have moderate-certainty indirect evidence supporting their safety and effectiveness in managing incomplete abortion and providing medical abortion. Direct evidence also supports their ability to assess gestational age using uterine size as part of manual vacuum aspiration provision. This option is feasible and could significantly improve equitable access to quality abortion care. Generalist and specialist medical practitioners are recommended to provide abortion care within their typical scope of practice. No additional evidence assessment was conducted for these roles. The World Health Organization (WHO) updated its recommendations to reflect evidence reviewed using the GRADE methodology. Recommendations for traditional and complementary medicine professionals, pharmacists, pharmacy workers, and CHWs were upgraded to recommend based on this review. For other health worker categories, recommendations remain unchanged. For managing incomplete abortion with vacuum aspiration, evidence supports the safety and effectiveness of traditional and complementary medicine professionals, auxiliary nurses, nurses, midwives, and associate clinicians. These roles are feasible and can increase access to care, particularly in low-resource settings. Health workers should not be required to report individuals suspected of unlawful abortion or provide incriminating information. Post-abortion contraception should be initiated as soon as possible, as ovulation can return within 8–10 days after an abortion. All contraceptive options may be considered, and the client’s preferences should guide the choice. For surgical abortion, contraception can be initiated at the time of the procedure. For medical abortion, hormonal contraception can be started immediately after the first pill of the regimen, while intrauterine device (IUD) placement should occur after confirming the abortion's success. Immediate initiation of depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) is associated with a slight decrease in medical abortion effectiveness but remains an available option. The WHO emphasizes integrating training and implementation of abortion-related tasks with basic emergency obstetric care (EmOC) services to improve access and continuity of care.
